Uplift of People Living Below Poverty Line 
† *381. SHRI P.K. MAHESHWARI : Will the PRIME MINISTER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether the target set by Government to bring the people above 
poverty line during the Eighth and the Ninth Five Year Plans could not be 
achieved; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) what effective steps are being proposed to be taken by Government to 
uplift of people living below the poverty line? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) No targets for bringing the people above the 
poverty line were set during the Eighth and the Ninth Five Year' Plans. 
However, the Ninth Five Year Plan has projected the percentage of people 
living below the poverty line to less than 5% by the end of the perspective 
period (2011-12). 
The Planning Commission estimates the percentage of persons living 
below the poverty line at national and State level from the 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
1 

RAJYA SABHA [22 March, 2001] 
sample surveys on consumer expenditure conducted by the National Sample 
Survey (NSS) Organization at an interval of approxim ately five years. These 
percentages are applied on the estimated population in order to arrive at the 
number of poor in the country. As per the latest available estimate, the 
number of persons living below the poverty line in 1999-2000 has been 
estimated as 260.25 million (26.10% of the total population) on the basis of 
the 30-day recall tabulation in the Key Results of the 55th Round large 
sample survey of Household Consumer Expenditure in India. 
(b) Does not arise. 
(c) There is a three-pronged action to alleviate and reduce the poverty in 
the country. These are: (i) acceleration of economic growth, (ii) human, and 
social development through literacy, education,   health,   nutrition,   meeting   
of   the   minimum   needs, 
elevation of social and economic status of the weaker sections of the society, 
etc., and (iii) direct attack on poverty through employment and income 
generating programmes and assets-building for the poor. 
The increase in income of the peopl e living below the poverty line occur 
from the joint impact of general growth process and direct income generation 
of the poor arising from various anti-poverty programmes introduced from 
time to time by the Government for their upliftment. Since the Sixth Five 
Year Plan (1980-85), the Government has been implementing employment 
and asset generation schemes for the upliftment of the people living below 
the poverty line. These schemes are mainly of two types, self-employment 
and wage employment. Integrated Rural Development Programme (IRDP) has 
been the major self-employment programme and it has been in operation in 
all the blocks of fhe country since 1980. The wage employment programme 
initially was National Rural Employment Programme (NREP) during the 
Sixth Plan period. In the Seventh Plan, another wage employment 
programme under the name Rural Labour Employment Guarantee 
Programme (RLEGP) was introduced. Then in 1989, Jawahar Rozgar Yojana 
(JRY) was launched by merging the National Rural Employment Programme 
and the Rural Labour Employment Guarantee Programme, and it 
2 

[22 March, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
became the main wage-employment programme. In addition, several 
programmes to help the poor were also in operation until March, 1999. 
These programmes are: Million Wells Scheme (MWS), Employment 
Assurance Scheme (EAS), Development of Women and Children in Rural 
Areas (DWCRA), Training of Rural Youth for Self-Employment 
(TRYSEM), Supply of Improved Toolkits to Rural Artisans (SITRA). 
From 1st April, 1999, these programmes, excepting EAS and JRY have 
been restructured into single sel f-employment programme called the 
Swamajayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY) with the primary objectives 
of focussed approach to poverty alleviation, capitalising advantages of group 
lending, and overcoming the problems associated with multiplicity of 
programmes. Also, from 1st April, 1999, Jawahar Rozgar Yojana (JRY) has 
been restructured as Jawahar Gram Samridhi Yojana (JGSY) with the 
primary objective of creation of demand driven community village 
infrastructure including durable assets at the village level and assets to 
enable the rural poor- to increase the opportunities for sustained employment. 
Its secondary objective is generation of supplementary employment for the 
unemployed poor in the rural areas. The wage employment under the 
programme is given to Below Poverty Line (BPL) families. 
From 1.12.1997, Swarna Jayanti Sahari Rozgar Yojana (SJSRY) is the 
main poverty alleviation programme in the urban areas. The SJSRY, which 
has subsumed all the earlier three urban poverty alleviation programmes, 
viz., Nehru Rozgar Yojana (NRY), Urban Basic Services for the Poor 
(UBSP), Prime Minister's Integrated Urban Poverty Eradication Programme 
(PMIUPEP), seeks to provide gainful employment to unemployed or 
underemployed urban and educated up to IX standard for setting up self 
employment ventures or provision of wage employment. The implementation 
of SJSRY is relying on suitable commun ity structures on the UBSP pattern 
and delivery of inputs under this programme is through the medium of Urban 
Local Bodies (ULBs) and such community structure.

Development of IT in Orissa 
*382. MISS FRIDA TOPNO: Will th e Minister of  INFORMATION 
TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have taken any step for development of I.T. in 
Orissa; 
(b) whether Orissa is lagging behind in the field of I.T.; and 
(c) if so, what steps Government propose to take to bring I.T. revolution 
in the State? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (SHRI PRAMOD 
MAHAJAN): (a) The Government of India have been assisting State of 
Orissa for development of IT in the areas of: 
(i) IT Education and Training  
(ii) IT Infrastructure and Connectivity 
(iii) E-Govemance 
Under IT Education and Training, Ministry of Information Technology 
society DOEACC has an operational counselling centre in Software 
Technology Park of India (STPI), Bhubaneswar for promotion of IT 
education in the State. Through DOEACC, variety of educational courses O, 
A, B levels are offered in the State for generating manpower. 
Under IT Infrastructure and Connectivity, STPI, is operating in 
Bhubaneswar providing satellite based data connectivity for exporting IT units. 
Recently, STPI has established a multi- purpose radio-mast to improve its 
services. A standby earth station is being planned by STPI for ensuring 
continuous data connectivity. Provision of two High Speed Data 
Communication (HSDC) facilities in Bhubaneswar in addition to STPI 
location are in planning stages. For cater ing to the IT industries dispersed in 
other parts of Orissa, a new STPI is being established at Rourkela. From STPI 
Bhubaneswar efforts of promoting IT sector, export growth of software to the 
tune of Rs. 137 crore were effected during 2000-2001 (40 per cent rise over 
1999-2000) and these are expected to grow further. 
4 

[22 March, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
Under E-Governance, Central Government has taken the initiative of 
organising meetings with State IT Secretaries and a National Conference of 
State IT Ministers. The conference of IT Ministers drawn up an action plan 
to promote IT and this is being followed up with the State of Orissa. 
(b) and (c) The State Government of Orissa has given priority to IT 
growth and has initiated many steps to promote IT. These coupled with the 
Central Government's efforts have enabled the State of Orissa to perform 
well in the IT sector compared to earlier. With many other initiatives from 
the Centre and State Government in the pipeline, the State of Orissa is poised 
for further growth in the field.

Track-H Deplomacy to solve Kashmir problem 
*385.  SHRI  GHULAM  NABI  AZAD:  Will  the  Minister of 
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Track-II diplomacy is in operation for solving 
Kashmir problem as reported by the Indian Press; and 
(b) if so, what are the main features of this policy? 
THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI JASWANT SINGH): 
(a) and (b) The term "Track II" is used in popular parlance, and in the media, 
to describe the exchanges between academics, scholars, journalists etc., from 
India and Pakistan. These meetings, which take place on a broad range of 
subjects, are of a private nature and do not have any official significance. 
The State of Jammu & Kashmir is an in tegral part of the Indian Union. A 
part of the territory of the State is under the forcible, and illegal occupation 
by Pakistan. Under the Simla Agreement and the Lahore Declaration, which 
are the cornerstones of India-Pakistan  bilateral relations, both India and 
Pakistan are committed to resolving a ll issues peacefully through bilateral 
discussions. Government have reiterated their commitment to resuming the 
Composite Dialogue initiated by India in 1998. An appropriate environment 
is an obvious requirement for a meaningful dialogue. For this, Pakistan must 
end its sponsorship of cross border terrorism and abandon hostile propaganda 
against India.

Cadre Review of the Indian Administrative Service 
*391. SHRI KHAGEN DAS: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether there is a system of cadre review of the Indian 
Administrative Service (IAS); 
(b) whether such a review is mandatory after a gap of five years; and 
(c) by when the next cadre review would take place? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF PERSONNEL 
AND TRAINING AND DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND 
PENSIONERS WELFARE OF THE MINISTRY OF PERSONNEL, 
PUBLIC GRIEVANCES AND PENSIONS (SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA 
RAJE): (a) and (b) Under the Cadre rules pertaining to the Indian 
Administrative Service, the Central Government is to ordinarily rc-cxamine 
the strength and composition of the IAS Ca dre of each State at an interval of 
every five years, in consultation with the State Government concerned. Such 
cadre reviews are not taken up for all the State cadres together, but are done 
individually for each cadre,  based on their requirements and the proposals 
received from the concerned State Government in this regard. 
(c) The dates on which cadre review s for each State of the IAS cadre 
were/are due are indicated in the Statement (See below). The Cadre reviews 
in respect of the AGMUT, Bihar and Jammu & Kashmir cadres have not 
been completed on the scheduled dates, as necessary proposals from the 
concerned State Governments/Cadre Controlling Authorities have not yet 
been received. The reviews will take place on receipt of proposals. Further, 
with regard to recently constituted St ates of Uttaranchal, Chhattisgarh and 
Jharkhand, it has been decided that the next cadre reviews in respect of the 
IAS cadre of these States would be taken up as and when the concerned State 
Governments come up with necessary  proposals, which may be 
14

due to take place on the Scheduled dates, after the receipt of required

encouraging the adoption of biotechnol ogy for the cultivation of medicinal 
plants and bamboo. The Department of Bio-technology, Ministry of Science 
& Technology and the Indian Council of Agricultural Research, Ministry of

plants.  Regeneration  protocols  have  been

national scale in either part of India is a matter of day to day; 
(b) whether Government have recently  announced the composition of

(c) if so, whether the Committee would hold its regular meetings regarding 
national disaster on State and Central level;

constant funding; and

provide requisite financial help on permanent basis? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE

the country is prone to various natural disasters.  Almost every year one part 
or other of the country

damage to infrastructure and private properties besides loss of human lives.

Salinity in Kutch area 
2863. SHRI YADLAPATI VENKAT RAO: 
SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether increasing salinity has spelt doom for thousands of 
fanners living in Kutch area on account of farm land becoming 
barren; and 
(b) if so, the assistance proposed to the poverty stricken farmers of 
the area who are migrating to towns in search of work? 
THE    MINISTER    OF   STATE    IN   THE    MINISTRY    OF 
AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHRIPAD YESSO NAIK): (a) and (b) Large 
number of farmers living in Kutch area have been affected by increasing 
salinity. The problem of salinity ingress in coastal areas of Kutch was 
examined by a High Level Committee constituted by the State Government 
under the Chairmanship of Shri K. Shivaraj, the then Chief Secretary, 
Government of Gujarat in 1978 and the committee recommended ingress 
control work worth Rs. 186 crores. 
37 

RAJYA SABHA [22 March, 2001] 
The Government of Gujarat in prin ciple accepted the recommendations in 
September, 1992 and the following works have been completed so far: 
i. One work of bund (Bandhara) completed. 
ii. One tidal ingress (Bharti control) work completed, 
iii. 101 check-dams constructed. 
iv. One reclamation bund work is in progress. 
So far, an expenditure of Rs. 13.80 cr ores has been incurred by the State 
Government in taking up these developmental works for saline ingress 
control in Kutch area.

Opening of new depots by DMS 
2865. SHRI GOPALSINH G. SOLANKI: 
SHRI BRATIN SENGUPTA: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) what is the number of new depots opened by the Delhi Milk Scheme 
during the last six months for sale of milk; 
(b) what was the sale of milk before and after opening of the said depots; 
(c) what is the amount of loss incurred by the Delhi Milk Scheme as a 
result of opening of new depot; and 
(d) what action Government propose to take against the officials 
concerned for opening of new depots and to curb such losses in future. 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(DR. DEBENDRA PRADHAN): (a) During the last six months DMS has not 
opened new depots of its own for sale of milk. However, 343 new sale points 
at shops, housing societies etc. have been started. 
(b) Approximately 18,350 litres of additional milk per day is being sold 
from these new sale points. 
(c) No losses have been incurred by DMS as a result of opening of new 
sale points. 
(d) Question does not arise in view of (c) above.

(a) what   is   Government's   reaction   to   the   news-item   which 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi.

appeared in the *Dainik Jagran' dated the 20th January, 2001 under the caption 
"Majbooran sasta dhaan bechne per kisano ko package ka laabh jald milne ke 
aasaar kum"; 
(b) whether Government propose to take any action and if so, the details 
thereof; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI SHRIPAD YESSO NAIK): (a) to (c) In order to reduce the hardship of 
farmers and to ensure procurement of paddy by the Food Corporation of India 
(FCI) and State Agencies the Government has extended the following 
concessions in Punjab during Kharif marketing Season 2000-01; 
(i) The procurement of paddy has been permitted with damaged, discoloured, 
sprouted and weevilled grains upto a maximum limit of 8 per cent instead 
of 3 per cent provided under the Uniform (FAQ) specifications; 
(ii) Paddy conforming to the above specification will be procured at the 
Minimum Support Price (MSP); 
(iii) Out turn ratio for custom milling of such relaxed paddy will be 64 per cent 
for raw and 65 per cent for par-boiled; 
(iv) It will be State Government's responsibility to get the paddy milled and 
deliver rice strictly conforming to the uniform specifications well within the 
current Kharif Marketing Season; and 
(v) It has also been agreed that the farmers of Punjab, whose paddy had 
been purchased at a price below MSP, the State Government would make 
good the difference. The expenditure arising out of this differential shall 
be restricted to a maximum of Rs. 100 crores. The Ministry of Finance shall 
compensate to the Government of Punjab for this expenditure to an 
extend of 50 per cent.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI SHRIPAD YESSO NAIK): (a) For increasing production and 
productivity of coconuts, the Coconut Development Board is implementing 
programmes for area expansion under coconut, production and distribution of 
quality planting material through regional coconut nurseries and Demonstration-
cum-Seed Production Farms established by the Board for hybrid seed 
production. The Board is also implementing programme on integrated

Agmark/ISI standards, fabrication and development of machineries for 
coconut processing, modernisation of coconut processing by introduction of 
improved dryers, techno economic surveys, consultancy services. For 
publicity and transfer of technology, the Board is bringing out publication in 
local languages, organising seminars, exhibitions, training programmes and 
workshops for the coconut growers and development officers of the States. 
The Board made an assessment of the effect of cyclone in 1996 and 1999 
in Andhra Pradesh and super cyclone in Orissa and submitted first hands 
reports to the Government. Appropriate plant protection measures were taken 
up after surveying and assessing the damage when incidence of mite was 
noticed in four southern States, for which funds were also released to

Price Stabilisation Policy 
2890. SHRI K. KALAVENKATA RAO: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be Dleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are in the process of working out a price 
stabilization policy (arrangement) to check rapid fluctuations in market 
prices of farm produce, particularly, that of cash crops; 
(b) if so, whether this would help the farmers; and 
(c) whether a final decision is expected in this regard and the likely benefits 
the farmers will get? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI SHRIPAD YESSO NAIK): (a) to (c) In order to stabilize prices of 
agricultural commodities, the Government is already implementing 
Agricultural Price Policy. The Government fixes each season the Minimum 
Support Prices (MSPs) for major agri cultural commodities. The MSPs are 
decided by using a methodology evolved over the years. The Government 
decides on the MSPs for various agricultural commodities taking into account 
the recommendations of the Commission for Agricultural Costs & Prices 
(CACP), the views of State Government s and Central Ministries as well as 
such other relevant factors, which in the opinion of the Government are 
important for fixation of the MSPs. Whenever prices fall below MSP level, 
the specified nodal agencies enter th e market and undertake procurement. 
For commodities not covered under MSP, Market Intervention Scheme 
(MIS) is under implementation having the same objective of price 
stabilization, instruments of trade are also being used to check fluctuation in 
domestic prices.

2959. SHRI K.B. KRISHNA MURTHY:  Will the Minister of LABOUR 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there has been growing tendency on the part of industrial 
houses and even Public Sector Undertakings to engage workmen on 'Contract 
Labour* basis; 
(b) whether according to the Industrial  Disputes Act in force, such 
workmen under 'Contract' labour are eligible for pay scale, perks and terminal 
benefits enjoyed by the regular workforce on company's/ PSU's direct 
payroll; and 
(c) whether Government have issued any directives to the labour 
contractors including the security agencies to extend the same facilities to 
their workmen including pay scales/per ks as applicable under the Minimum 
Wages Act and the ID Act? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (SHRI 
MUNI LALL): (a) to (c) The Governme nt is aware that there has been 
reported increase in engagement of contract labour. The Contract Labour 
(Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 has been enacted primarily with a view 
to safeguard the rights and privileges of the contract workers and prevent 
their exploitation. 
The Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Central Rules, 1971 
provides under Rule 25(2)(v)(a) that  the wages and other conditions of 
service of contract labour shall be the same as that of regular employees if the 
contract workers perform the same or similar nature of work. In the light of 
the ruling of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Air India Statutory Corporation 
vs. United Labour Union and Others in December, 1996, the establishments 
engaging contract labour in a process/work/job are under an obligation to 
absorb contract   labour   on   regular   basis   wherever   the   "Appropriate 
179 

RAJYA SABHA [22 March, 2001] 
Government" by way of notification made under Section 10 of this Act have 
prohibited engagement of contract labour in such process/ work/job in those 
establishments. 
The provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act apply to workers appointed 
on contract basis directly by the Principal Employer whereas the Contract 
Labour (Regulation & Abolition), Act 1970 applies to contract workers 
engaged through a contractor or subcontractor. The licensing authorities 
while granting a licence to the contractors bring to their notice the provisions 
of the Act and the rules with regard to wages and other facilities to be 
extended to the contract labour as a condition of the licence.

Number of people below poverty line 
† 2970. PROF. MM. AGARWAL: Will the PRIME MINISTER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the number of people living below poverty 
line in rural areas of the country is not declining even after fifty years of 
independence; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether Government have taken so far any policy decisions under the 
national agenda in this regard; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) The estimat es of the incidence of rural 
poverty made by the Planning Commission from the large sample surveys on 
consumer expenditure conducted by the National Sample Survey 
Organization (NSSO). The percentage of people living below the poverty 
line in rural areas declined from 56.4% in 1973-74 to 37.3% in 1993-94 and 
the number of people below the poverty line in rural areas declined from 
261.3 million to 244.0 million during the same period. On the basis of the 
30-day recall tabulation in the Key Results of the 55th Round large sample 
survey of Household Consumer Expenditure in India carried out by the 
NSSO, 193.24 million of the rural population (27.09% of the total rural 
population) lived below the poverty line in 1999-2000. 
(b) Does not arise. 
(c) and (d) There is a three-pronge d action to alleviate and reduce 
the poverty in the country. These are: (i) acceleration of economic 
growth,   (ii)   human,   and   social   development   through   literacy, 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
195 

RAJYA SABHA [22 March, 2001] 
education, health, nutrition, meeting of the minimum needs, elevation of 
social and economic status of the weaker  sections of the society, etc., and 
(iii) direct attack on poverty through employment and income generating 
programmes and assets-building for the poor. 
The increase in income of the people living below the poverty line occur 
from the joint impact of general growth process and direct income generation 
of the poor arising from various anti-poverty programmes introduced from 
time to time by the Government for their upliftment. Since the Sixth Five 
Year Plan (1980-85), the Government has been implementing employment 
and asset generation schemes for the upliftment of the people living below 
the poverty line. These schemes are mainly of two types, self-employment 
and wage employment. Integrated Rural Development Programme (IRDP) 
has been the major self-employment programme and it has been in operation 
in all the blocks of the country since 1980. The wage employment 
programme initially was National Rural Employment Programme (NREP) 
during the Sixth Plan period. In the Seventh Plan, another wage employment 
programme under the name Rural Labour Employment Guarantee 
Programme (RLEGP) was introduced. Then in 1989, Jawahar Rozgar Yojana 
(JRY) was launched by merging the National Rural Employment Programme 
and the Rural Labour Employment Gu arantee Programme, and it became the 
main wage-employment programme. In addition, several programmes to help 
the poor were also in operation until March, 1999. These programmes are: 
Million Wells Scheme (MWS), Employ ment Assurance Scheme (EAS), 
Development of Women and Children in Rural Areas (DWCRA), Training 
of Rural Youth for Self-Employment (TRYSEM), Supply of Improved 
Toolkits to Rural Artisans (SITRA). 
From 1st April, 1999, these programmes, excepting EAS and JRY have 
been restructured into single self-employment programme called the 
Swamajayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY) with the primary objectives 
of focussed approach to poverty alleviation, capitalising advantages of group 
lending, and overcoming the problems associated with multiplicity of 
programmes. Also, from 1st April, 1999, Jawahar Rozgar  Yojana  (JRY)   
has  been   restructured  as  Jawahar  Gram 
196 

[22 March, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
Samridhi Yojana (JGSY) with the primary objective of creation of demand driven 
community village infrastructure including durable assets at the village level 
and assets to enable the rural poor to increase the opportunities for sustained 
employment. Its secondary objective is generation of supplementary 
employment for the unemployed poor in the rural areas. The wage employment 
under the programme is given to Below Poverty Lines (BPL) families. 
From 1.12.1997, Swama Jayanti Sahari Rozgar Yojana (SJSRY) is the main 
poverty alleviation programme in the urban areas. The SJSRY, which has 
subsumed all the earlier three urban poverty alleviation programmes, viz., Nehru 
Rozgar Yojana (NRY), Urban Basic Se rvices for the Poor (UBSP), Prime 
Minister's Integrated Urban Poverty Eradication Programme (PMIUPEP), seeks to 
provide gainful employment to unemployed or underemployed urban and 
educated up to DC standard for setting up self employment ventures or 
provision of wage employment. The implementation of SJSRY is relying on 
suitable community structures on the UBSP pattern and delivery of inputs under 
this programme is through the medium of Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) and 
such community structure.

Development in NE States 
2974. SHRI SWARAJ KAUSHAL: Will the PRIME MINISTER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that developmen t in North-Eastem States has not 
been commensurate with huge allocations given by the Central Government 
during the last few decades; 
(b) if so, what steps Government have taken to ensure optimum utilization 
of the financial assistance; 
 
(c) the Planning Commission has devised some criteria that indicates the 
financial discipline followed by the North-Eastem States; and 
(d) if so, the finding thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING (SHRI 
ARUN SHOURIE): (a) and (b) Development of a Region depends on a large 
number of factors, such as natural potential, availability of funds; and 
effective delivery machinery.  It is fact that the North-Eastern States have 
been given liberal plan as sistance by the Government  of India. As against 
their share of 3.74 per cent in the tota l population of the country, these States 
were given a share of 19.30 per cent in Central assistance by the Planning 
Commission in 1999-2000. Ninety per cent of the plan assistance to these 
States is grant and only 10 per cent is tr eated as loan, as against 30 per cent 
grant and 70 per cent loan for other St ates. In addition, the North-Eastem 
States are also being given non-plan grants from the Ministry of Finance as a 
result of recommendations of the Eleventh Finance Commission to cover 
their non-plan deficit. 
200 

[22 March, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
Despite such liberal assistance, eco nomic growth of the North-Eastern 
States has not been as good as in  other States. The Table shown at 
Statement-I (taken from the Economic Survey, 2000-01) i ndicates that the 
percentage increase in the Net State Domestic product over the period 1993-
94 to 1998-99 has generally been less for the NE States as compared to other 
States ((See below). 
3. However, it should be kept in mind that the NE States suffer 
from several constraints, some of them are beyond their capacity to 
rectify, at least in the short or medium term, such as 
• Poor connectivity 
• Geographical isolation 
• Inadequate infrastructure 
• Less developed formal credit 
• Poor quality of land and low agricultural yields 
• Little inflow of private capital 
• Industrial backwardness, and 
• Insurgency 
 
4. Moreover, as opportunities for employment to the educated youth are 
extremely limited because of inadequa te development of the secondary 
sector, Governments in these States have provided public employment to a 
very large number of people. This has resulted in massive increase in pension 
and salary payments, especially after the acceptance of the Fifth Pay 
Commission Report in 1997. 
5. The adverse impact of these factors on economic development and 
asset creation has been exacerbated by  weak delivery structures in these 
States. However, it is primarily for th e State Governments to take remedial 
action for better implementation. Planning Commission has on several 
occasions drawn the attention of the State Governments to improve its 
implementation capacity and achieve sustainable growth. As an extreme 
measure, Planning Commission has recently asked the Ministry of Finance to 
stop release of further instalments of Central assistance to Manipur where 
unauthorized diversion of funds had taken place.

(c) The Planning Commission has recently undertaken a Review of posts 
in the light of the guidelines of the Mi nistry of Finance and as an outcome of 
the Review, 157 posts at various levels have already been abolished in the 
Planning Commission during the year 2000-2001. Besides, a number of posts at

(d) In the face of changing domestic  economic policy regime and an 
equally fast paced integration of the economy with the emerging global order, 
investment planning is no more the only, or the more predominant, or even the 
most effective instrument of pursuing development. In fact, the role of State and 
hence of planning has to move from a direct intervention in economic activity 
in general and the production process in particular, to facilitating creation of 
an environment that encourages individual initiative and reaches out by 
providing opportunity to all. Planning has to, therefore, go beyond undertaking 
mere budgetary allocations, between the competing   sectors   and   regions,   for   
that   alone   would   not   be

enough, and move towards ensuring policy harmonisation over time and 
across space. This requires the Planning Commission to strengthen its role as 
a "Think Tank"—a repository of expert knowledge. 
Planning Commission is currently engaged in an exercise to determine 
what would be the most effective role for the Commission in the altered 
domestic and global scenario. In this regard, a note prepared on the Role of 
the Planning Commission in the wake of changing economic scenario was 
discussed in the full Planning Commission Meeting held on 30th September, 
2000 under the chairmanship of th e Prime Minister. The proposal was 
broadly approved and is to be further discussed between the Deputy 
Chairman and the Union Finance Minister.

ARUN SHOURIE): (a) to (c) The Major Self-Employment   Schemes   
implemented   in   the   country   including

(SGSY)   in   rural   areas,   Swam   Jayanti   Shahri   Rozgar  Yojana

and Prime Minister's Rozgar Yojana (PMRY). The SGSY covers all aspects 
of self-employment, viz. organization or rural poor into self-help groups and 
their capacity building, planning of activity clusters, infrastructure build up, 
technology, credit and marketing. In urban areas SJSRY seeks to provide 
gainful employment to urban unemployed or underemployed poor by 
encouraging the setting up of self-employment ventures or provision of wage 
employment. Under the margin money scheme of REGP proposals are 
submitted by entrepreneurs to various banks/financial institutions for setting 
up village industry units. The PMRY aims to provide employment/self-
employment to educated unemployed youths. For the North Eastern Region 
the scheme has been recently (1998-99) revised by raising the age limit to 40 
years, income limit upto Rs. 40000 per annum and by covering all viable

Criteria for Developing NH 
† 2996.   SHRI   LAJPAT   RAI:   Will   the   Minister  of  ROAD 
TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of the criteria and the basis on which Government are 
constructing and developing National Highways; 
(b) whether any uniform policy is being adopted by Government 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
229 

RAJYA SABHA [22 March, 2001] 
for all the States; 
(c) whether Government have carried out a study regarding the deplorable 
condition of the National Highways in Jharkhand, Uttaranchal and 
Chhattisgarh and whether these National Highways exist only on the papers; 
and 
(d) if so, the details of those found responsible for this condition? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ROAD 
TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS [MAJ. GEN. (RETD.) B. C. 
KHANDURI] : (a) The Central Government does not normally construct new 
National Highways. It takes over suitable State roads and converts these to 
National Highways based on the criteria laid down for the purpose as per 
statement annexed (See below). Development of National Highways is a 
continuous process and works are taken up based on the condition of the 
road, traffic volume, inter-se-priovity and overall availability of resources. 
(b) Yes, Sir. 
(c) No such study has been carried out. However,, the entire National 
Highway network in the country including in Jharkhand, Uttaranchal and 
Chhattisgarh is generally kept in traffic worthy condition within the available 
resources. 
(d) Does not arise. 
Statement 
The criteria for the declaration of State road into National Highway is as 
under:— 
(i) Roads which run through the length and breadth of the country. 
(ii) Roads connecting adjacent countries. 
(iii) Roads connecting the National Capital with State capital and roads 
connecting mutually the State capitals. 
(iv) Roads connecting major ports, large industrial centres or tourist 
centres. 
230 

[22 March, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(v) Roads meeting very important strategic requirements. 
(vi) Arterial roads which enable sizeable reduction in travel distance 
and achieve substantial economic growth thereby. 
(vii) Roads which help opening up large tracts of backward area and 
hilly regions. 
(viii) National Highway grid of 100 Km. is achieved. 
(ix) The road must be upto the standard laid down for State 
Highways—both in its technical requirements as well as the land 
requirements. 
(x) The road and right of way must be free of any type of 
encroachment and should be the property of the State. 
(xi) The right of way required for the National Highway (preferably 45 
m, minimum 30 m) must be available for acquiring, free of 
encroachment and the State Government would complete acquiring 
formalities within six months. 
NB: The declaration of National Highways is considered based 
on the requirements of the country as a whole and not particularly 
with respect to any local requirements.

3008. SHRI SOLIPETA RAMACHANDRA REDDY: Will the PRIME 
MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Andhra Pradesh Government has requested the Central 
Government to consider the measures for promoting satellite based 
communications in the country;

240

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF SPACE 
(SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE):  (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Andhra Pradesh Government had suggested the following 
measures for promoting satellite based communications in the 
country: 
(i) Permit use of Ku-band from any satellite system suitable for 
communications including data services by licensed enterprises. 
(ii) Expedite clearances and permissions to license private agencies to 
set up international internet gateways using any available satellite 
system with the least expensive transponder capacity. 
(iii) Permit State Governments and private sector enterprises to uplink 
educational TV programmes and information services etc., from 
Indian territory, subject to sp ectraj clearance from the Wireless 
Adviser. 
(iv) Permit the satellite communications sector the same investment 
limit in respect of foreign equity as allowed for telecom sector. 
(v) Treat the hardware requirement for satellite communications on 
the same footing as for the Information and Telecommunication 
sector for purposes of import duties and tariffs to encourage 
Complete Knock Down (CKD)/Semi Knock Down (SKD) 
manufacturing locally. 
(c) and (d) These measures have to be assessed in the context of 
the systems currently operational in the country and the purposes for 
which they are being put to use.

Delayed Projects 
3011. SHRI   P.   PRABHAKAR   REDDY:   Will   the   PRIME 
MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news-item 
captioned "189 Government projects face delay" appearing in the 'News-
Time* dated the 9th January, 2001; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether any steps have been in itiated to identify the persons 
responsible for the reported time and cost overruns; 
(d) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor; and 
(e) what measures Government propose to take to ensure that projects are 
completed as per the schedule and within the sanctioned Budget? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF STATISTICS 
AND PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) 
and (b) As on 1.1.2001, out of 197 ma jor and mega projects each costing Rs. 
100 crores and above, 128 projects have  cost overrun of the order of Rs. 
46,082.7 crores and 91 projects have time overrun with respect to their 
original schedule of commissioning. The sector-wise break-up of cost 
overruns as well as time overrun is given in the enclosed statement (See 
below). The reasons for delay are lack of supporting infrastructure facilities; 
delay in finalisation of detailed engineering and release of drawings and 
delay in availability of fronts; changes in scope; industrial relations and law 
& order problems; delay and uncertainty in feedstock supply; 
precommissioning teething troubles; technology problems; and geological 
surprises. 
(c) and (d) In order to bring accounta bility in the execu tion of projects, 
Standing Committees have been set up in all the concerned 
243 

RAJYA SABHA [22 March, 2001] 
Ministries/Departments, for projects co sting Rs. 50 crores and above, which 
have reported time & cost overruns. These Committees are headed by 
Additional Secretary or Jo int Secretary of the concerned Ministry with 
representatives from Planning Commission, Department of Expenditure and 
Ministry of Statistics & Programme Implementation. The Standing 
Committees set up as per the guidelines of the Planning Commission issued 
in August, 1998, have the mandate to go into the details of time and cost 
overrun and to identify the respective responsibility areas and to suggest 
remedial action. The reports of the Standing Committees form part of the 
revised cost estimates of projects which have time and cost overruns and the 
same are submitted, along with the no te for consideration of the Cabinet 
Committee on Economic Affairs. Identification of individuals responsible for 
such time and cost overruns forms part of the action taken report of the 
concerned Ministry/Department on the recommendations of the Standing 
Committee. 
(e) The measures taken to complete the projects as per schedule are as 
follows: 
(i) review of projects on monthly as well as quarterly basis by the 
Government; 
(ii) Indepth critical review of th e progress by the Project Authorities 
and the administrative Ministries and follow up with the State 
Governments (for acquisition of land and provision of 
infrastructure facilities like water and power, ensuring law & 
order at project sites, etc.), consultants and other concerned 
agencies to minimise delays; 
(iii) setting up of an Empowered Committee in the concerned 
administrative Ministries for resolution of problems; 
(iv) bringing modifications in the Land Acquisition Act and 
Rehabilitation Packages; 
(v) inter-ministerial coordination for resolving problems of inter-
ministerial nature;

(vi) making available matching funds to complete the projects in the 
advanced stages of implementation along with the revised 
completion schedule; and 
(vii) reviews by the Minister-in-char ge,  the Prime  Minister's Office 
and the Cabinet Secretariat.

Area Development Scheme (MPLADS) is passed by the Parliament annually

the Winter Session of the Parliament and was made available to this Ministry 
thereafter. This amount was also nearly exhausted by the middle of February, 
2001. The eligible cases for release of funds had to be kept pending between 
October, 2000 and January, 2001 and once again after the middle of 
February, 2001. Request for another supplementary grant of Rs. 250 crore 
has been made to the Ministry of Finance. The release of funds will again 
start once the supplementary grant is provided to this Ministry.
